n: God renews the very first blessing of Genesis 1 to Noah’s family. Noah becomes like a second Adam, the father of a renewed human race.

f.w: Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth

n: The relationship between people and animals changes. Animals will now fear humans, and humans are given authority over them—a stewardship that carries responsibility.

f.w: the fear of you and the dread of you
f.g: A new reality after the Flood: animals will be wary of people.

n: For the first time God explicitly permits people to eat animal flesh, just as He had earlier given plants. Latter-day revelation adds that meat is to be used sparingly and with thanksgiving.

f.g: Food.

f.w: Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you

n: One limit: they must not eat meat with its blood. Blood represents life, which belongs to God. This principle runs through the law of Moses and points to the sacred blood of Christ.

f.w: the life thereof, which is the blood thereof

n: God will hold every creature and person accountable for taking a human life. The JST adds that animals’ blood must not be shed wastefully either.

f.g: Will demand an accounting for. JST Genesis 9:10-11 adds that blood should not be shed except for food to save life, and warns against wasting flesh.

n: Murder is the gravest offense because every person bears God’s image. The verse is crafted as a poetic mirror: shed—blood—man / man—blood—shed.

f.w: in the image of God made he man

n: God repeats His command to have children and fill the earth. The renewed world is meant to teem with life again.

f.g: Literally “swarm,” as living things did at creation (1:20).

n: God now speaks to Noah and all his sons together, introducing His covenant.

f.g: The covenant includes all of Noah’s descendants—all humanity.

n: God Himself makes the covenant. It is His initiative and His promise, extending to future generations.
Remarkably, the covenant also includes every animal. God’s promises reach to all living things.
The promise: never again will a flood destroy all life on the earth. Latter-day scripture teaches that the earth’s future cleansing will be by fire, not water.

f.w: neither shall there any more be a flood

n: God gives a visible sign of His covenant, one that will last through all generations.

f.g: A sign or reminder of the covenant.

n: God places the rainbow in the clouds as the sign. The Hebrew word for bow also means a warrior’s bow—some see God hanging up His weapon in peace.

f.g: Hebrew qeshet — a rainbow, but also an archer’s bow.

n: Whenever storm clouds gather, the rainbow will appear as a comforting sign.

f.w: the bow shall be seen in the cloud

n: God says He will remember His covenant. The rainbow reminds God as well as people—an image of His faithfulness.
The JST adds that when God looks on the bow He will remember the covenant made with Enoch: that in the last days Zion would return and the earth would rejoice.

f.g: JST Genesis 9:21-25 links the rainbow to God’s covenant with Enoch that Zion would return.

n: God repeats that the rainbow is the sign of His covenant with all life—three times in a few verses, for emphasis.

f.w: This is the token of the covenant
f.g: The repetition seals the promise.

n: Noah’s three sons are named, with a note that Ham is the father of Canaan—setting up the next story and later Israel’s relationship with the Canaanites.

f.g: Ancestor of the Canaanites, who lived in the land later promised to Abraham.

n: All the earth’s peoples descend from these three sons. The next chapter traces their families in detail.

f.g: Scattered and populated.

n: Noah becomes a farmer and plants a vineyard—the first vineyard mentioned in scripture.

f.g: A farmer; one who works the soil.

n: Noah drinks too much wine and lies exposed in his tent. Scripture honestly records the failings of even great prophets.

f.g: Some Latter-day Saint readers note that the JST does not remove this event.
Exposed; lying uncovered.

n: Ham sees his father’s shame and tells his brothers, apparently making a mockery of it rather than protecting his father’s dignity.

f.w: saw the nakedness of his father
f.g: The exact nature of Ham’s wrong is debated; at minimum it was disrespect and exposing his father’s shame.

n: Shem and Japheth respectfully cover their father, walking backward so as not to look. Their actions model honoring parents and protecting others’ dignity.
Noah wakes and learns what Ham had done.

f.g: Possibly “youngest”; Ham is usually listed second, so the phrase may mean “lesser” or refer to Canaan.

n: Noah curses Canaan, Ham’s son, to be a servant. Historically this foreshadows Israel’s later dominance over the Canaanites. The Church has firmly disavowed past ideas that used this curse to justify racism.

f.g: The curse is on Canaan specifically, not on all Ham’s descendants or any race.
A Hebrew way of saying “the lowest of servants.”

n: Noah blesses the God of Shem. Through Shem will come Abraham, Israel, and ultimately Jesus Christ.
Japheth will be enlarged—his name sounds like “enlarge”—and will dwell in Shem’s tents, sharing in Shem’s blessings. Many see a hint that other nations would one day share Israel’s covenant.

f.g: Wordplay: Japheth (yefet) and “enlarge” (yaft).

f.w: dwell in the tents of Shem

n: Noah lives 350 years after the Flood—long enough, by the Bible’s numbers, to overlap with Abraham’s early life.

f.g: By Genesis chronology Noah died about two years before Abraham’s birth, or later by some reckonings.

n: Noah dies at 950. With his death, the line of the pre-Flood patriarchs closes. Latter-day revelation teaches that Noah stands next to Adam in priesthood authority.
